\section[\bn{নমস্কার}]{\bn{নমস্কার} (nômoshkar) — \textquotedblleft{}hello\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:BN-C01-nomoshkar}



\begin{quote}
The first Bengali word — and it hides the single sound-shift that makes Bengali \emph{Bengali}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(If you already read Bengali, skim this.)} Bengali runs \textbf{left to right} under a top line; every consonant carries a built-in vowel — but in Bengali that vowel is \textbf{ô} (an open \textquotedblleft{}o\textquotedblright{}), \emph{not} \textquotedblleft{}a.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\bn{ন}} nô, \textbf{\bn{ম}} mô, \textbf{\bn{ক}} kô, \textbf{\bn{র}} rô. A \textbf{vowel sign} changes it (\textbf{\bn{া}} ā); a \emph{hasanta} under \textbf{\bn{স্}} strips its vowel so it joins the next as a conjunct: \textbf{\bn{স্} + \bn{ক} $\to$ \bn{স্ক}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{নমস্কার}} is the \emph{same word} as the Sanskrit \emph{namaskāra} behind Hindi's and Marathi's greeting — \emph{namas} (\textquotedblleft{}a bow\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{kāra} (\textquotedblleft{}the making of\textquotedblright{}). But hear what Bengali does: the inherent \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{} becomes \textbf{ô}, and \emph{s} shifts to \textbf{sh}, so written \emph{namaskāra} is spoken \textbf{nô·mosh·kar}. That habit — \emph{a$\to$ô}, \emph{s$\to$sh} — is Bengali's fingerprint; once you hear it, you can un-shift almost any word back to its Sanskrit cousin.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\emph{Nômoshkar}, palms together, is the everyday respectful greeting — hello and often goodbye — the broad, secular-to-Hindu default in Bengal. Bengali is the language of Tagore, the only tongue to have written the national anthem of \emph{two} countries: India and Bangladesh.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item read it — nô · mosh · kar
  \item the two shifts that made \emph{namaskāra} into \emph{nômoshkar} (a$\to$ô, s$\to$sh)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Sanskrit word is \emph{nômoshkar}, and what two Bengali sound-shifts disguise it? (\emph{Namaskāra}, \textquotedblleft{}the making of a bow\textquotedblright{}; the inherent \emph{a$\to$ô} and \emph{s$\to$sh}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\bn{ধন্যবাদ}]{\bn{ধন্যবাদ} (dhônyobad) — \textquotedblleft{}thank you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:BN-C01-dhonnobad}



\begin{quote}
The same \textquotedblleft{}thank you\textquotedblright{} Hindi, Marathi, and Punjabi use — now watch Bengali reshape it \emph{twice}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
New: \textbf{\bn{ধ}} dhô (a breathy \emph{d}), \textbf{\bn{ব}} bô, \textbf{\bn{দ}} dô, and the conjunct \textbf{\bn{ন্য}} (\textbf{\bn{ন}} n + \textbf{\bn{য}} y). With the \textbf{\bn{া}} sign, read \textbf{\bn{ধ}·\bn{ন্য}·\bn{বা}·\bn{দ}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{ধন্যবাদ}} = Sanskrit \emph{dhanya} (\textquotedblleft{}worthy\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{vāda} (\textquotedblleft{}a saying\textquotedblright{}) — the very \textquotedblleft{}thank you\textquotedblright{} behind Hindi \emph{dhanyavād}. Two Bengali quirks fire at once: the inherent \emph{a$\to$ô} again (\emph{dhônyobad}), and — because Bengali has \textbf{no separate \textquotedblleft{}v,\textquotedblright{}} only \textbf{\bn{ব}} \emph{b} — Sanskrit \emph{vāda} is spoken \emph{bad}. \emph{V} becoming \emph{b} is a Bengali signature (think \emph{Bishnu} for \emph{Vishnu}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
This is the standard, slightly formal thanks. In warm everyday speech Bengalis often lean on the whole gesture and tone rather than the word — but \emph{dhônyobad} is what you say and write when you mean it plainly. Note how much you already knew: only the \emph{sound} changed, not the roots.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item read it — dhô · nyo · bad
  \item the two shifts hiding \emph{dhanyavāda} here (a$\to$ô, v$\to$b)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Dhônyobad} comes from which two Sanskrit parts, and why is the \textquotedblleft{}v\textquotedblright{} gone? (\emph{Dhanya} \textquotedblleft{}worthy\textquotedblright{} + \emph{vāda} \textquotedblleft{}saying\textquotedblright{}; Bengali has no \textquotedblleft{}v,\textquotedblright{} only \emph{b}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\bn{হ্যাঁ} / \bn{না}]{\bn{হ্যাঁ} / \bn{না} (hyã / nā) — \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:BN-C01-hyan-na}



\begin{quote}
Two words no conversation survives without — and one is an old cousin of English.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
New: \textbf{\bn{হ}} hô, the \emph{y-phola} \textbf{\bn{্য}} that glides the sound, and the nasal mark \emph{chandrabindu} \textbf{\bn{ঁ}} — a little moon-with-dot that sends the vowel through the nose. \textbf{\bn{না}} is simply \textbf{\bn{ন}} + \textbf{\bn{া}}, \emph{nā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{হ্যাঁ}} (\emph{hyã}, \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{\bn{না}} (\emph{nā}, \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}). That \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} rides the ancient negative \textbf{na-} — the same Proto-Indo-European \emph{ne} behind English \textbf{no}, \textbf{not}, \textbf{none}, Latin \emph{nōn}, and Hindi \emph{nahīṇ}. Bengali kept it at its shortest, bare \emph{nā}: the family resemblance to English \emph{no} sits right on the surface.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The \emph{chandrabindu} (that nasal moon-dot) is everywhere in Bengali and gives the language part of its soft, nasal music. Hear the breath leave through the nose at the end of \emph{hyã} — that mark is doing the work.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item read them — hyã / nā
  \item the shared ancestor of Bengali \emph{nā} and English \emph{no} (PIE \emph{ne)}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the \emph{chandrabindu} do, and what links Bengali \emph{nā} to English \emph{no}? (It nasalises the vowel; both descend from Proto-Indo-European \emph{ne, \textquotedblleft{}not.\textquotedblright{})}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\bn{আচ্ছা}]{\bn{আচ্ছা} (āchchhā) — \textquotedblleft{}okay / I see\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:BN-C01-achchha}



\begin{quote}
The little word that keeps every Bengali conversation moving.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
New: \textbf{\bn{আ}} — the \textbf{independent} vowel \emph{ā}, the shape a word uses when it \emph{starts} with a vowel. (A built-in vowel rides a consonant; a standalone one gets its own letter.) Then the doubled \textbf{\bn{চ্ছ}} (\textbf{\bn{চ}} \emph{ch} + \textbf{\bn{ছ}} \emph{chh}). Read \textbf{\bn{আ}·\bn{চ্ছা}}, \emph{ā-chchhā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{আচ্ছা}} (\emph{āchchhā}) is the all-purpose \textquotedblleft{}okay, alright, I see, go on\textquotedblright{} — a true workhorse of spoken Bengali, from Sanskrit \emph{acchā} (\textquotedblleft{}good, clear\textquotedblright{}). It is the word a Bengali speaker peppers through speech the way an English speaker says \textquotedblleft{}right… right,\textquotedblright{} a nod made audible.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Note it opens with \textbf{\bn{আ}}, a \emph{standalone} vowel-letter — your first. This is the other half of how the script handles vowels: attached to a consonant they are little signs (\textbf{\bn{া}}), but on their own they stand as full letters (\textbf{\bn{আ}}). Same sound, two shapes, chosen by position.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item read it — ā · chchhā
  \item why \bn{আ} is written in full here (the word starts with a vowel)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{āchchhā} do in conversation, and why is its first vowel a full letter, not a sign? (It means \textquotedblleft{}okay / I see / go on\textquotedblright{}; a word-initial vowel takes its standalone form \textbf{\bn{আ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\bn{আসি}]{\bn{আসি} (āshi) — \textquotedblleft{}I'll be going\textquotedblright{} (goodbye)}

\label{lesson:BN-C01-ashi}



\begin{quote}
Bengalis do not say \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving.\textquotedblright{} They say \textquotedblleft{}I'll come again.\textquotedblright{} Here is why.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
New: \textbf{\bn{স}} again — here truly \textquotedblleft{}sh\textquotedblright{} — and the \textbf{\bn{ি}} sign (\emph{i}), which in Bengali is \textbf{written before} the consonant it follows but \textbf{read after} it. \textbf{\bn{আসি}} = \textbf{\bn{আ}} + \textbf{\bn{সি}}, \emph{ā-shi}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{আসি}} (\emph{āshi}) literally means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I come},\textquotedblright{} from the verb \emph{āsā} (\textquotedblleft{}to come,\textquotedblright{} a Sanskrit root shared with Hindi \emph{ānā}). Yet it is how Bengalis say \emph{goodbye} — never \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving\textquotedblright{} (unlucky, too final) but \textquotedblleft{}I'll come {[}again{]}\textquotedblright{}: \textbf{\bn{আসি}}, or the fuller \emph{āschhi} (\textquotedblleft{}I am coming\textquotedblright{}). It is the very same \textquotedblleft{}promise of return\textquotedblright{} farewell Tamil and Marathi reach for — a whole culture's optimism folded into one verb.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
And notice: \emph{āshi} is \textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{} whether a man or a woman says it — Bengali marks \textbf{no gender on the verb}. That sets it apart from Marathi (\emph{yeto} m. / \emph{yete} f.) and, in this one respect, makes Bengali's verbs simpler than its neighbours'.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item read it — ā · shi (remember \bn{স} = \textquotedblleft{}sh\textquotedblright{})
  \item what \emph{āshi} literally means and why it means goodbye (\textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}I'll come again\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does \textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{} mean goodbye in Bengali, and what does Bengali \emph{not} mark on this verb? (Saying \textquotedblleft{}I'll come again\textquotedblright{} avoids the finality of \textquotedblleft{}leaving\textquotedblright{}; no gender.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 1 — Practice and Recall}

\label{lesson:BN-C01-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Just the five, mixed and recombined — and the one shift that ties them together.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{How to answer — rapid recall}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hello / goodbye, palms together — \emph{nômoshkar}
  \item thank you — \emph{dhônyobad}
  \item yes and no — \emph{hyã} / \emph{nā}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}okay, I see, go on\textquotedblright{} — \emph{āchchhā}
  \item goodbye, \textquotedblleft{}I'll come again\textquotedblright{} — \emph{āshi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — the one habit}]
Bengali's fingerprint. Un-shift these back to the Sanskrit you know:

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item what is \emph{nômoshkar} in \textquotedblleft{}un-shifted\textquotedblright{} Sanskrit? (\emph{namaskāra})
  \item what became of the \textquotedblleft{}v\textquotedblright{} in \emph{dhônyobad}? (Bengali has no \textquotedblleft{}v\textquotedblright{}; \emph{vāda} $\to$ \emph{bad})
  \item the inherent vowel of every Bengali consonant — \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}ô\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{ô})
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — roots you now carry}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item inherent vowel \textbf{ô} + \emph{s$\to$sh} + \emph{v$\to$b} = the Bengali sound-fingerprint
  \item \emph{nā} (\textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}) $\leftrightarrow$ English \textbf{no / not / none} (PIE \emph{ne)}
  \item \emph{āshi} (\textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{}) = the \textquotedblleft{}promise of return\textquotedblright{} goodbye, shared with Tamil \& Marathi
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A friend parts by saying \emph{āshi}, and you want to answer warmly. What does \emph{āshi} really mean, and what could you say back? (\textquotedblleft{}I'll come again\textquotedblright{} — you can answer \emph{āchchhā, āshi} — \textquotedblleft{}okay, I'll come {[}too{]},\textquotedblright{} returning the same optimism.)
\end{tcolorbox}
